extracted.intended_audience: stonemasons, monument conservators, architects, cemetery managers, and municipal engineers responsible for outdoor monuments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting, evaluating, and siting monumental stone (marble, sandstone, granite, flagstones) for outdoor use in town/churchyard environments, including diagnostics of weathering processes and expected rates of decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: White marble unsuited for out-of-door use in polluted moist towns
rubrics_metrics.description: White marble is here utterly unsuited for out-of-door use, and its employment for really fine works of art meant to stand in the open air in such a climate ought to be strenuously resisted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations show white statuary marble exposed in a moist, coal-smoke town climate is largely destroyed within a century; superficial solution and internal disintegration can render inscriptions illegible and the stone pulverulent (examples from Edinburgh churchyards). Avoid using white statuary marble for outdoor monuments in similar climates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gypsum (sulphate of lime) crust formation is protective but deceptive
rubrics_metrics.description: A pellicle of amorphous gypsum (sulphate of lime) is deposited upon marble, inclosing soot/dust particles and producing a dirty gray to brown-black crust that preserves the even surface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crust retards superficial solution so inscriptions may remain legible while the interior is disintegrating; microscopic/chemical tests (sulphur reaction) identify it. However, when the crust cracks or blisters and is broken, rapid disintegration of the underlying stone follows. Monitor crust condition; its presence can mask serious internal decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal disintegration from carbonic acid in rainwater
rubrics_metrics.description: Disintegration of marble is mainly due to the action of carbonic acid in permeating rainwater, which partially dissolves crystalline granules and destroys mutual adhesion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This process occurs in all exposures and can be distinctly traceable in tombstones less than twenty years old; it leads to loss of cohesion so that a slight pressure crumbles the stone to sand. Use this diagnostic (crumbly sand beneath crust) to assess internal decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure to rain and site orientation strongly affect weathering rate
rubrics_metrics.description: The rate of transformation of monumental stone depends primarily on the extent to which it is exposed to rain; slabs sheltered by projecting architraves or less directly exposed retain inscriptions much longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When siting or evaluating monuments, consider orientation (facing direction), overhangs, and local wind-driven rain patterns. Examples: NE-facing, well-sheltered slabs retain legibility for a century or longer; exposed faces decay faster.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tightly-fitted slabs in rigid frames risk curvature and fracture
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble slabs firmly inserted into a solid framework and placed erect or horizontal often bulge (center swelling) and develop fractures and rents due to internal expansion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a slab is tightly jammed between a sandstone frame there is little room for expansion and the center will swell outward, producing wave-like curvature and fractures (rents proceeding inward from margins). Where possible, avoid rigid, tight fixing that prevents expansion or allow movement/expansion space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freeze-thaw (frost) expansion is a principal cause of internal swelling/curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble is porous and imbibes water; when interstitial water freezes its expansive force increases granule isolation and stone dimensions, producing the observed swelling and fractures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In climates with recurrent frost, prefer less-porous, frost-resistant materials and avoid porous marbles for outdoor use. Expect accelerated internal breakdown from repeated freeze-thaw cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sandstone selection: prefer nearly-pure fine silicious sandstones without bedding
rubrics_metrics.description: The best sandstones consist of nearly pure fine silicious sand, with little or no iron or lime, and without trace of bedding structure; when properly selected they are remarkably durable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select sandstones with high silica content (examples with ~98% silica performed well over centuries). These resist weathering far better than porous, lime- or iron-bearing varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sandstones containing a soluble or easily removable matrix (clay, carbonates, iron oxides)
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a soluble/easily removable matrix (clay, carbonates of lime and iron, anhydrous/hydrous iron peroxides) causes rapid disintegration of arenaceous rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject stones showing these matrices; documented cases show inscriptions lost in decades and measured surface losses of about three fourths of an inch per century where such impurities occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stones with distinct laminae/stratification for exposed faces; 'lay on its bed'
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a sandstone is marked by distinct laminae of stratification it is nearly certain to split along these lines under weathering if bedding planes are directly exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Builders should 'lay a stone on its bed'—avoid setting laminated sandstones on their edge for exposed inscriptions or decorative work. Thinly-bedded flagstones set on edge will peel off in successive layers and are unsuitable for upright inscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condemn blocks containing concretions or pyritous inclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Concretionary masses of different composition or texture weather at different rates and can hollow or project; pyritous concretions decompose to produce sulphuric acid and dark stains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any block showing such concretions—especially pyrite-bearing material—should be unhesitatingly condemned for architectural/monumental use; such impurities cause unsightly disfigurement and rapid localized decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagstones and thinly-bedded stones are unsuitable when used on edge for inscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Flagstones (thinly-bedded sandstones) set on edge are particularly prone to lamination and scaling, removing large portions and destroying inscriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using flagstones set on edge for inscribed monuments; prefer thicker, massive stones or proper orientation to preserve inscription durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granite and syenite: generally durable but limited long-term data; polished surfaces may weather faster
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental plates of syenite and granite showed slight annual loss; polished granite sometimes lost more than rough surfaces and polish may disappear over decades, but satisfactory long-term comparative data are lacking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Granite is promising for outdoor monuments but may not surpass best silicious sandstones in permanence; consider surface finish (polished may weather differently) and acknowledge limited long-term evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measurable indicators (surface lowering, curvature) to project remaining life
rubrics_metrics.description: Rates of weathering can be quantified (examples: ~1/3 inch / century by superficial solution; in cases of internal displacement curvature up to 2.5 inches in ~40 years and total disruption within ~100 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure surface lowering, curvature, and the presence/extent of rents/blisters to estimate rate of decay and remaining lifespan; use historic examples to calibrate projections for similar stone and exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crust cracking patterns (polygonal cracking, blisters, curling) are diagnostic of imminent rapid decay
rubrics_metrics.description: The crust may crack into a polygonal network; polygons may curl up or rise in blisters—when these rupture the underlying stone is rapidly exposed to disintegration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspect for cracked crust, blisters, and curling polygons; their presence indicates that protective crust is failing and that rapid internal disintegration will follow once the crust is breached. Conservators should prioritize such stones for intervention or replacement.
